utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I had communicated with the parties by e-mail yesterday afternoon indicating the Prosecution wished to make submissions with respect to the late disclosure of the proofing note and additional documents we received on Saturday afternoon prior to the witness beginning his testimony. I wonder if I may be permitted to do that at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this something that would prohibit the witness from making solemn declaration itself?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I had just thought it might be preferable to do it before the witness took the declaration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So is the thing that you wanted to make that submission in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It doesn't matter at all, Your Honour, in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then we'll have the witness make his solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And would the counsel representing the witness introduce himself to the Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I am Stephane Piletta-Zanin, I represent or, rather, I will assist Mr. Galic during his testimony. Would you like me to add anything? Let me precise [as interpreted] that I will be speaking French, as usual, in this courtroom, and I hope that you will bear with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. [In English] I take it, Mr. Galic, that Mr. Piletta-Zanin explained this to you. However, before you commence your evidence, I must draw your attention -- do you hear me in your language, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard you, but it was not in a language that I understand because I speak Serbian. Now I can hear interpretation into Serbian and it will be all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Before you commence your evidence, General Galic, I must draw your attention to a certain Rule of procedure and evidence that we have here at the International Tribunal, that is Rule 90(E). Under this Rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, from the Prosecution, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt in a -- for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that your answer will incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in such situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you save and except for -- except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, General Galic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Galic. Now the Chamber will hear you, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'd just like to put some observations on the record, and it's with, as I indicated previously, with respect -- this is a notice issue, and this is with respect to the late notice of the material which is a 15-page very detailed proofing note and 12 additional untranslated documents, three maps, only one of which was already exhibited, which were delivered or e-mailed at 5.27 p.m. on Saturday night. And, Your Honours, that's well less than 48 hours before General Galic was expected to testify, and in that regard I would say in specific contravention of the guidelines Your Honours set in place for the procedures for the conduct of this trial. And this set of documents, Your Honours, that we received on Saturday was actually the third set identified that might be used in the course of the examination-in-chief of General Galic. The first, about 65 in number, we received on the 27th of March, the second, 107, we received on the 9th of April, and of course we welcome in advance the documents because even though they don't tell us what General Galic might say in his testimony in chief, we've been working with them to try and identify themes that might be the subject of his testimony, and we do that because without an adequate summary of specific facts on which the General is expected to testify, that's all we have. The General's summary, his 65 ter summary for two years of command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was 11 lines long. And -- but looking at those documents, Your Honour, with rare exception, the documents that we received before Saturday only seemed to relate largely to one paragraph on page 7 of this summary, in fact the second full paragraph on page 7, which relates to Muslim attacks. Now, when you look at those -- the greater number of those documents against the summary, it looks like the Prosecution actually has been wasting their time in preparation for this examination-in-chief, wasting our time out of court and not saving it, and it's put us in effectively the worst of all possible scenarios because we're coming into an examination on some areas of evidence in that summary cold. And just looking at the summary that we received on Saturday, I also note that there's areas on here that weren't even close to being identified in the 65 ter summary as filed. There was no notice that General Galic would speak about the SRK before he arrived. There was no notice that he would speak about its place in the VRS. There was no notice that he would speak about UNPROFOR and the UNMOs. There was no notice he would speak about the relationship with civilian authorities, no notice that they would speak about the media, no mention that they would speak about proportionality and selectivity of fire. Your Honours, of course the Prosecution's been able to guess or anticipate that some of those might be the subject of testimony, but not a word of that has been mentioned in the summary, and the documents have actually -- I would go as far as to say sometimes led us down some rabbit holes when we could have been directing our preparations on or into the actual information that the General might testify to. The way this has gone actually undermines our ability to effectively cross-examine General Galic. But now keeping in mind that it appears as though there's going to be some breaks during the course of the examination-in-chief this week, and of course with the undertaking that we're going to do our utmost best not to waste the Court's time, I hope we will be prepared to cross-examine on all areas, but given the lateness of this notice, Your Honours, when the time comes, I feel I may be addressing you with respect to certain areas of the evidence mentioned during the examination-in-chief in that we might require additional time to prepare on those areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, very briefly. We thought of all these things last year when we asked the Chamber to bring the witnesses who were serving their sentences in other locations to The Hague earlier because the Registry wouldn't appoint them counsel, so we couldn't have any proofings until they got here and the Prosecution opposed that request and persuaded the Chamber that it was only necessary for the witness to be here one week before they commenced their testimony. As a result of that, we didn't have a chance to obtain any information from General Galic until he arrived here last week. Since then, we've done our best to provide the Prosecution with, as they say, a detailed proofing note, which I wonder if they prefer we didn't give them such a detailed proofing note, but in any event, we've done our best to inform them of the substance of General Galic's testimony as soon as we became aware of it. If they need more time to prepare for their cross-examination when the time comes, which probably will not be until the beginning of next week, we certainly wouldn't have any objection to that, but I think this is a little bit of the boy crying wolf. Ms. Edgerton prosecuted General Galic, worked on his case for three or four years.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, she attended the trial, let's put it that way, or participated in the trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, then I'm mistaken about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please do not overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I apologise [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Now you realise at which pace we should proceed. Please continue, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise if that's not correct, but nevertheless, the Prosecution prosecuted General Galic, thousands of documents were dealt with in his case, and they had a full range of information about his conduct. So to claim at this stage that they're not prepared to cross-examine him is a little overblown in our estimate, but nevertheless, we remain committed to assist the Prosecution in not having to commence its cross-examination until it's reasonably prepared. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes. Does the Prosecution have anything to add? Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Only to clarify, if it's necessary to do so, that the suggestion, perhaps inadvertent, that the Prosecution brought this problem on itself, that is not at all the case. The Prosecution's position in respect of the first time the issue of the arrival of previously convicted witnesses arose was consistent with the Trial Chamber, and that was based on the idea that members of the trial team could go to where the witness was well in advance and prepare that witness. Now, apparently that normally expected procedure foundered on the issue of appointment of counsel, at least in the previous case. When that happened, I met with Mr. Robinson and indicated to him that in light of that problem, the Prosecution would fully support any remedial steps that would address the problem that had arisen. So -- and nothing in the interim that took place to prevent the situation we find ourselves in now notwithstanding our positions of support for anything that would do so. So I'm only addressing at this moment the suggestion that somehow we brought this on ourselves. We did not. This is a very significant problem, as one can imagine, and the -- the emphasis on the volume of material available that Mr. Robinson just made is precisely the problem. The preparation could go in many, many, many different directions and expend -- and require the expenditure of enormous resources, which is precisely why the rules provide for detailed factual summaries, proofing notes and other forms of guidance to narrow the area of preparation required by the opposing party, and that's the nature of the problem. And as Ms. Edgerton indicated, notwithstanding enormous efforts by Ms. Edgerton and other persons assisting her in an effort to prepare, we suddenly find ourselves confronting issues that were not notified and for which adequate preparation was not undertaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, would you like to add anything, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While I note that all these problems originally originate from the insufficient summary of the witness, the Defence 65 ter list, I appreciate the Prosecution's commitment to do its utmost not to waste the court time. So if necessary, the Chamber may consider deferring the cross-examination of the witness about certain issues. Thank you. Then, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General Galic.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, I must ask you and remind myself that we should speak at a moderate pace and make a break between question and answer so that everything may be recorded. General, could you briefly say your full first and last name and your father's name.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: My name is Stanislav Galic, lieutenant-general of the Army of Republika Srpska, and my father's name is Dusan. I have been retired since --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll get there. Tell us, please, your date and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: The 12th of March, 1943, at Golesa in the Banja Luka municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: I'm a prisoner now in Freiburg, and that's my occupation as it were. It's not a profession, but it's an occupation. It's what I do now, and I must do my time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that you were a retired lieutenant-general; right?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm a retired lieutenant-general of the Army of Republika Srpska, and a major-general of the Army of Serbia. It may be illogical, but I'm sure you understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please list briefly the stages of your education.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: I graduated from primary school in Banja Luka. Then I continued my education in the military system, which began in 1950, and that took longer than ten years in different time periods. I graduated from the non-commissioned officers' school in Sarajevo. Then I graduated from the military academy in Belgrade and the Command Staff Academy in Belgrade as well as the school of All People's Defence in Belgrade. That would be my education in a nutshell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are these all the schools or courses that you need to finish to become a general?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Well, these were the schools, but to become a general you need much more. You must get good assessments. You must work well in your position, and there were other criteria to become a general in the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. Until you become colonel, you will be promoted in the regular fashion, but after that there were ethnic quotas. There were quotas to consider the ethnic composition of Yugoslavia for becoming a general.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you explain to the Chamber from what that originates and what the result of that quota was?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Well, there were various results. One of the results was that all the ethnicities in Yugoslavia were represented, and that's positive, of course. But at a certain point in time, due to that quota, some people would become generals who were maybe not best prepared. Since the Serbs were the -- were the most numerous ethnicity in Yugoslavia, most generals were also Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us which positions you were in until you arrived at the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: To put it briefly, I was in every position from platoon commander to corps commander, company commander, battalion commander, regiment or brigade commander, division commander, and finally corps commander. I retired as corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During your career were you commended, decorated, or rewarded?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: You couldn't become general if you weren't commended, rewarded, and decorated. So I received some of these during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Can you tell us where you were, in which position, before you joined the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Before joining the SRK, I was commander of the 30th Infantry Division at Mrkonjic Grad, which is in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was its zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Well, the zone changed depending on the certain period of time. Initially it encompassed the area of Drvar and so on, all the way up to Glamoc, and in depth up to Kljuc and Petrovac. Later on, when the 2nd Corps arrived, it took over this zone and the division remained deployed in the area towards Kupres, and then later on that part was also excluded from the division area such as Mrkonjic Grad and Jajce and Knezevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When were you appointed or, rather, when did you join the SRK and which post did you have?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: I joined the SRK on the 10th of September, 1992, and I took up the position of the corps commander. I have to add, though, you know that posts are taken voluntarily with the consent of the general. In this situation, however, lots of things were not clear sufficiently, but I nevertheless accepted this post.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your predecessor, the previous commander of the SRK, when did he leave his post, and what was the situation in the corps upon your arrival and the situation in the theatre of war?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when General Sipcic left the position of the commander, but I think that was more or less a month before my arrival. I don't know exactly. At that time there was a directive issued by the Federal Secretariat of National Defence of Yugoslavia before the formation of the VRS that all those who were not born in Bosnia-Herzegovina or had no specific orders to that effect were not required to remain where they were. They were able to be transferred to other areas, for example, to Montenegro. Since I was born in Bosnia-Herzegovina, of course I remained there. As for Sipcic, I assume when he acquired the rank of the general decided to go to Belgrade, and as far as I know, he never came back and I think he retired there. Now, what did I find as far as the situation was concerned. I found a corps without the commander and without the Chief of Staff of the corps. You remember when you met me at Jahorina when I was taking over my duty, you would recall that the situation in the corps was quite complex, and I don't know whether we should go into details regarding the complexity of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Hopefully we shall come to that. A minute ago you said -- but can you tell us whether a corps commander is higher than the division commander?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Well, the corps commander is a higher position than the division commander, although they are approximately the same with regard to the authority. Division has less authority, and therefore the commander can be either a colonel or a general. So that would be the difference. And the strength is lesser, and I'm talking about the division, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So if one was transferred from a division to the level of a corps, would that be considered as a promotion?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You just said that people accepted this voluntarily but that in your case it seems as if you didn't go there voluntarily. Can you give us the reasons why the position of the SRK commander was not so desirable to you?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Well, there were several reasons, but the main one was the complexity of the very theatre of war of Sarajevo, because that was one of the most difficult one within the whole theatre of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There is a witness who said many times that waging war in Sarajevo, equally for commander or a soldier or a civilian, was simply a nightmare, and I think that it speaks for itself. I think that we shall deal with other characteristics at later stage regarding this particular theatre of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the composition of the SRK, and how many lower-level units were included in it?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Well, mainly when I arrived we had nine light brigades. We had a mixed anti-armour regiment, a mixed armour artillery regiment. We had a light artillery regiment. We had a battalion, communications battalion, medical battalion, and transport battalion, and communications battalion if I omitted to mention that. So those were more or less the units that made up the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. That was the situation prevailing until the 1st of November, 1992. After that, two brigades left the corps so that the corps was sort of downsized at that time. That would be in brief the strength and the composition of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the occasion and which specific brigades had left the SRK, and where were they transferred?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: The two brigades that left were the 1st Romanija and the other one, and they joined the Drina Corps that was established at that time. The other one was the Rogatica Brigade. One part of armoured and mechanised units also went away because this was a newly established unit that was formed on the 1st of November, 1992, and it became operational at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any changes in the area of responsibility as a result?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Well, it affected the zone of responsibility, because practically the zones of responsibility of these brigades went as far as the Drina, the Drina River, and towards Kladanj and Olovo, but now the zone was slightly changed, but we expanded it in another direction. So after these two brigades left, we gained the Nisic plateau direction and the part that was held by the 2nd Romanija Brigade. The rest remained within the zone of responsibility of the corps, the one within Sarajevo itself, then the area towards Jahorina and Igman mountains, and other directions and axes which I can name if you wish me to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, did we understand you correctly when you said that after the departure of these two brigades they did not change the area of responsibility, only these two zones were excluded from your area?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between questions and answers and speak more slowly. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's very difficult for the interpreters to catch up with your speed unless you put a pause between the question and answers and speak very slowly. Mr. Galic, could you repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to the zones of responsibilities of those two brigades, if a unit leaves and they left the SRK, they became part of the Drina Corps, and, of course, their respective zones of responsibility were not under the SRK jurisdiction any longer but they were transferred under the jurisdiction of the Drina Corps. That would be my answer, if I repeated it properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You made -- mentioned the Rogatica Brigade called after its municipality. Can you tell the Chamber the brigades that remained within the SRK, what kind of formations were they? What were their zones of responsibility, and in what way were they connected with their respective defence areas?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: The remaining part of the brigade or the remaining part of the corps, everything was based on the territorial principle. Initially, the municipality took care of those brigades themselves because that was a form of self-organisation by the people themselves. Until the 19th of May, all of that was part of the JNA. We know that the Serbian people advocated the option of remaining within Yugoslavia, that the task of the Yugoslav People's Army was to defend the sovereignty and integrity of Yugoslavia, and as a result, they were more linked to the JNA. It didn't pay much attention to other things which left them not sufficiently prepared for the new situation that emerged post-19th of May. Now we have the Ilidza Brigade which was mostly deployed in the area of Ilidza and was holding positions towards Stupska junction in Nedzarici, towards Dobrinja, Alipasino Polje, and of course this area is facing the airport as well. Now, the next part of the front line was towards the Mount Igman, Stojicevac and other places, but the Igman mountain itself was held by the BH Army. It is interesting to say that the area of this brigade, particularly the area of Nedzarici, were constantly surrounded or semi-surrounded as it were. So for a person to be a commander there was an extremely difficult task. I had to go there on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I please ask you to show us that on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 65 ter 24947.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You can also use the map that is on the screen, but I believe that we and the other parties concerned will have --

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, yeah -- now I have a very small map on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If it would be more convenient and easier for you, can someone give you a pointer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just to note that this was one of the potential exhibits that was notified on Saturday night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow the point. This is --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Notified late.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thursday or Friday shouldn't be considered as belated notice. We sent this to them on those two days and we asked them to scan the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Specifically what problem do you have with using this map, Ms. Edgerton? It's difficult to follow what kind of problem it may cause.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: At the moment, none for the Prosecution, Your Honour, just to make a note when we come to the time of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's proceed. If necessary we can zoom in, but I don't know how far we can zoom in, but I leave it to you, Mr. Karadzic, how to proceed with the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I trust that we can enlarge the central part, because there's a lot of empty space on the sides of the map. So we can zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, if it is easier for you to use the map behind you and to make a presentation for the benefit of the Chamber so that they can follow both. You were talking about the Ilidza Brigade, so could you please be kind to tell us where its zone was, where its neighbouring units were, and where the positions of the enemy in front of it were.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: When I was discussing -- microphone. How -- you'll hear me. When I was discussing the positions of the Ilidza Brigade, these are the positions, and they are marked in colour blue, and this is the area of Nedzarici, Nedzarici, Alipasino Polje, the settlement, Aerodromsko settlement, Dobrinja. So this was the area where Nedzarici itself was. These red lines indicate the position of the Army of BH. Blue lines indicate the positions of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Usually we always indicate our own forces with colour red. So if we were -- if this had been --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please wait for the interpretation to be finished.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would it be easier for the General, Your Honours, to use a pen to indicate the positions on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't think it will be easy for me because this map is not clear. I can't see almost anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I find it a bit difficult to follow the way in which the witness is indicating on the map, because it's difficult to recap his evidence. If you'd zoom in part and part, and if necessary he can mark it. We can admit it in several pieces if necessary. Think about the matter. Or the General can explain the map as it is described on the map with the zoomed-in map. Shall we try that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I think that's the best solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, can you please go back to the desk, and then we shall ask the Registry to zoom in the bottom left part of the map grid.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we zoom in further, please. There is quite a bit of the outlying area that we don't need. Can we enlarge it a bit further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, is this an appropriate view now?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I will now indicate exactly where the Ilidza Brigade had its positions. It manned the positions of Aerodromsko settlement. We can see how the blue line stretches. Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you place the letter A with your electronic pen to indicate the airport settlement, Aerodromsko settlement?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: This is just one portion of it here. It's not working really well, is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You can erase this, perhaps, and just put an ordinary A. Or you can put numbers if you prefer.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Yes, numbers would be better.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then 1 for Aerodromsko settlement.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: There, it's done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And to the north of Aerodromsko settlement?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Yes, Nedzarici. We can place number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please go on and introduce to us the area of responsibility of that brigade.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: In this area of Nedzarici and Aerodromsko settlement there was only one battalion of the Ilidza Brigade. The other battalion manned Stup and the Stup junction here. So that's the area around here. That would be number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, number 3 is fine.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: It also mans the positions around Energoinvest. So this is the Stup area. And this bit is interesting, as we come to the area of Otes. That area was, until the 10th of December, 1992 -- and that would be number 4; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Number 4.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: I can't read the lettering at all, so I'm just placing this from my memory, and if I make a mistake, please take this into consideration. So this area was, up until the 10th of December, 1992, under the control of the BH Army. Subsequently, it was under the control of the SRK forces, that's to say of the Ilidza Brigade, through to the Dobrinja River. We can see the river here. It's the Dobrinja, which stretches along almost the entire front.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you draw a line to indicate the flowing of the Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Well, all right. I think you can see it anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, sir, can you tell the Chamber who was opposite the brigade in the various stretches of the line?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Let me first round off just the area of the brigade, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: This brigade also had positions opposite Stojicevac. We'll mark it with number 5. We can see that all the way down in the south, it's the 4th Motorised Brigade that held its positions. That's Stojicevac, across from the airport. It also manned the positions in the direction of Mount Igman all the way to Golo Brdo, Golo hill, which you can't see in the map, but it's opposite Otes. This was an area of 800 metres only. The entire brigade was, in fact, in an encirclement or semi-encirclement during that period of time. That was why it was necessary to go out into this area in the direction of Otes to round this up and to prevent Golo hill from being captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Then in the direction of the Mount Igman can you just place an arrow and say that it indicates the direction of Golo hill and place number 6.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Well, Golo Brdo is basically one of the hills of Mount Igman. Is this all right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Number 6 and an arrow.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: I am not really good at handling this pen, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, starting from Otes and then further on eastward, who is the enemy really there?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: It changed in this area. This map reflects the situation as it was at the time I took up my positions. That's the Motorised Brigade. And we held this area of Alipasino Polje, which we could mark with number 7. That's the Alipasino Polje neighbourhood. Is that right? Is number 7 all right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: This area was held by the 101st Mountain Motorised Brigade, and in the direction of Dobrinja, it was the 5th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Number 8, please.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Number 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, can you tell us first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we stop here. Shall we ask the witness to date and put his initials onto this map. Today is 15th of April, 2013. Probably top right, at the top right part of the map, could you date and initial. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I wonder if I could ask one further thing, Your Honour. Perhaps we could have for the record the date of the map --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's why I'm going --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- I'm asking the witness to save this at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If I were to introduce a map, I would introduce the provenance and the date of the map it was produced. While after we kept this into the record, why don't you put those questions to the witness, Mr. Karadzic. Could you put the date, Mr. Galic, on the map, at the top right part.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today's date?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. 15th of April. And your initials, please, or signature.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. We keep this as --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is one other thing I would like the witness to mark, please, so I'd like to have something marked before we admit it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, tell us what were the features that were held by this Motorised Brigade? What was the population?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: In the area of responsibility of the 3rd Motorised Brigade in relation to Ilidza and the area of Stup junction, there was this one specific feature which was a silo next to the Stup junction, and it was out of there that most of the activity aimed at Ilidza came from. The rest were mostly high-rise buildings and that especially applies to the area in the direction of the Nedzarici, the students' centre, Alipasino Polje, Dobrinja, because Nedzarici is mostly single housing, family houses, whereas around Nedzarici you had high-rise buildings, skyscrapers. Across the Miljacka, there is the area under the 2nd Motorised Brigade. That's the Brijesce Brdo, Brijesce hill, and you can see the area under the control of the Ilidza Brigade from the vantage point of Brijesce hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you place number 9 to indicate Brijesce hill. Yes, it's right. It's been interpreted well. Can you place number 9 on Brijesce hill.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: I don't see where it is written on this map so I'm just going to place it from my memory. I think this would roughly be where Brijesce hill is located.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you also identify where Mojmilo is and how it is related to and in what position does it stand in relation to the other neighbourhoods.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Mojmilo is east of the 5th Mountain Motorised Brigade, and it is under the control of the 101st Brigade. This is where Mojmilo is situated roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Number 10, please.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Thereabouts. Dobrinja is up there, and then Mojmilo would be over here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And finally, General, this portion of the map that we will now admit, which map does it belong to, and who drew the map?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: This portion of the map was taken from, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You can look behind your shoulder.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: It's taken from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. We'll keep it as a temporary next Defence exhibit. We'll keep it, and let's zoom in on the top left corner of the map. Shall we designate as an MFI -- temporarily mark it for identification. What's the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI 3381, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The upper left-hand corner is what we need to identify the provenance of the map. It will be on your screen shortly. Can we zoom in on the upper left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have it, not yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Upper-left corner of the map, same map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Further to the left. Yes, now I have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We do not need the witness to mark the map at the moment. Yes. Please go ahead. We can zoom in a bit further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, can you tell the Chamber what is the stamp that has been affixed here?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's the stamp of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, would you like this zoom to be admitted as well? And the General can place his signature on it, we will know that the previous portion comes from this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, it's not necessary. We can zoom in at any moment. I would ask the witness to read out this portion in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. "Operational map of the staff of the 1st Corps. Beginning --" or, rather, first I should say that there's a stamp beneath it of the command of the 1st Corps. And then it reads: "Beginning: 1 December 1992. End: 4 April 1993." That's all that we can read here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And bottom left part. Scroll down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here we have the legend or the key indicating the situation as it was in different periods of time, and we will see that they differ slightly from the situation as it was at the beginning and at the end. And the first one is the 1st of December, 1992. The next line is the 4th of December, 1992. Then the 9th of December, 1992. Next, the 11th of December, 1992; 14th December 1992; 15th December 1992 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's now sufficient. When did you see this map for the first time, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw this map for the first time at my trial. I think that it was being shown repeatedly by the Prosecutor until we started putting certain questions about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any objection to the admission of this map, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No. We're just looking to see if it was actually used in the Galic trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we need a translation for this map or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't think so. It's been read into the record, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Do you have any observation to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I consider myself as the owner of this map that I have brought here in order to facilitate things. I'm still working on this map, and there is a problem because I would like to have the original of the map. I think that people have been informed about this, so there shouldn't be any problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What does a BBR mean, Mr. Galic, in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] BBR, Mountain Brigade. MTBR stands for Motorised Brigade. If you're interested, I can tell you what it all means. MBR stands for Mechanised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I think we have a proper basis to admit this.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it was P467 in the Galic trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll admit the entire map into a new Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3382, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the previous one we admitted as marked for identification, Exhibit D3381, will be admitted in full. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have D3381 again so that the General can speak about the strength and structure of the enemy based on that map. D3381.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, General, can you tell us what were the reasons, military or otherwise, for you to capture Otes?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: The taking of Otes had a typically military reason. I explained that Otes and Golo hill, which were both held by the BH Army, were blocking the Ilidza Brigade from exiting from that zone. It is important to add that we failed to mention an important feature, and that's the airport, which at the time was controlled by UNPROFOR. Probably there will be questions about this so that we'll probably get back to this. This had a military reason, and I can elaborate, if you want, about Otes. It's very interesting that when I arrived when -- we immediately established contact with the people on the opposite side. The Ilidza Brigade informed all civilians that it would try to take Otes, and some civilians who wanted to move out of that area, and they were mostly Croats, and I'm not sure of the ethnic composition of those who were transported to Kiseljak, but it was several dozen. They -- there were a number buses who took them there. Then the fighting for Otes began. This was a new housing development made of reinforced concrete, and many people were killed, even the brigade commander, I mean the Ilidza Brigade, Zoran Borovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please explain to the Chamber what forces the enemy had opposing the Ilidza Brigade, that is, the 3rd Motorised Brigade? What kind of forces did they have, and what kind of equipment?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Basically their brigades numbered about 2.000 men. Here in this area they had mortars, infantry weapons, and they had support from Igman and other parts of town. If they needed it, they could get support from the howitzers at Igman and even by a 130-millimetre gun that was there. But as far as I know, the BH Army did not target this area with their artillery, but they used all the other weapons they had. And the mortars moved a lot. They also had many rifle brigades --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Rifle grenades.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They had a lot of those, because they manufactured them. And here in this area there were also snipers, in all these high-rise residential buildings. From Alipasino Polje through the students' settlement, all the way to the Stup junction, all the building -- in all the buildings there were snipers. In Sarajevo, as far as we knew, there were some 500 snipers in all, that is, sniping rifles. Whether they got any more, I don't know, but the number was thereabouts. In the area of this brigade we can only make an assessment of their numbers because they changed. And then they engaged the special units like the Swallows or the Larks and others that have been mentioned here before this court. If necessary, I can go into -- I can elaborate more on these units. Furthermore, they were occasionally supported by a tank, but I wasn't -- I didn't get any information about that in the reports I received. There was a howitzer battalion somewhere around Humsko hill, and the armoured battalion, that's what they called it, was somewhere around the brickworks and the railway station, and they went up to Zuc -- Zuca or toward the threatened directions. They manoeuvred with their forces. Wherever there was a threat, they would manoeuvre with their forces and engage their forces fast and efficiently. There was strong fire from Igman on the Ilidza Brigade. They even used barrels filled with explosives and nails or what have you. Of course, when that explodes, it had a devastating effect. I don't know if I elaborated sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't quite understand because of the length of the answer. I was wondering if we're still talking about the 3rd Motorised Brigade or if we've gone on to talk about other units. I'm unclear. Because the question was about the 3rd Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I can explain. I asked the General to explain who the opponents of the Ilidza Brigade were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, ask the witness to clarify what he said instead of you giving testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, we're speaking about only the 3rd Motorised Brigade or about all brigades, including the 101st and the 5th, opposing the Ilidza Brigade?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: In principle I spoke about all brigades in Sarajevo, and I described their composition. I also described the composition of the 3rd Motorised Brigade and what significant things there were. Just like the other units that opposed the Ilidza Brigade, because we cannot look at one brigade and its actions in isolation, because it never acts in an isolated manner. It's part of a corps that is a system so that the 3rd Brigade and the 101st and the 5th, just as the 4th and the 8th Brigades from Igman and so on, act in a synchronised fashion toward Ilidza. So we cannot look at only one brigade. But I've outlined the specific features of the others too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So those were the brigades opposing the Ilidza Brigade, the 8th from Igman, the 3rd, the 101st, the 5th, and the 4th. The 5th from Dobrinja and the 4th from Hrasnica; right?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Yes. They opposed the Ilidza Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us now what kind of weapons they had at Hrasnica, for example, or what did the 101st have to face the Ilidza Brigade toward Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Their weapons. Well, I said that they had all kinds of infantry weapons. I especially stressed the fact that they had many sniping rifles from which -- which they had deployed on high buildings and all high features, such as hills, around the Ilidza Brigade. Then there were mortars. And at Mojmilo, and I watched it personally, there were also some recoilless guns belonging to the 101st at the time and the 5th -- all right. Well, there was some overlap there, but there was a recoilless gun there. And they also fired -- fired rifle grenades. And when I went to Nedzarici, I was only able to go there at night. You couldn't go there in daytime because they would target you with all sorts of weapons. When I went there, I saw that the situation was really very difficult, and even today we must praise those fighters as heroes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where were those fighters at Nedzarici for [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: All the fighters at the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps were local soldiers. Those are people from Nedzarici, Ilidza, or some people from the other parts of Sarajevo. That was the composition mostly of those forces at the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, including Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To what extent did commanding such a unit differ from commanding a professional military unit?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Well, there are many differences. I was a professional soldier, but basically the goal is always the same. The differences, however, are the following: That personnel was insufficiently trained for house-to-house fighting. Not only were those soldiers poorly trained for such combat, but the rest of us, even the professionals, were poorly trained for this kind of fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll get there yet. Can you tell us what kind of weapons the 4th Brigade at Hrasnica had, I mean the BH Army? I don't mean the artillery at Igman but at Hrasnica itself. Did they target you and with what kind of weapons?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: There was fire by the Ilidza Brigade from Hrasnica, to be more precise, from Stojicevac. They fired from all sorts of infantry weapons and then there were mortars. They also had also had some other weapons including sniping rifles, quite a few, and this brigade didn't differ much from -- from the other brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned manoeuvre. Which forces of theirs manoeuvred? What kind of assistance did come to this area? Which units intervened?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: It was mostly those free forces, to call them that, and by that I mean special forces. Then there were these special brigades who for a while were at the disposal of the corps, and then there were groups that were established from Vikic's group to the Swallows, to the Larks. And that reinforcement was such that it was very difficult to fight them off. And often they would use parts of one -- some units from one brigade to transfer to another brigade if there was a threat there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And on page 28, you said "mobile mortars," and it was interpreted as mortars that moved. What exactly did you mean?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: In Sarajevo, the parts held by the BH Army, it was characteristic that they had mortars mounted to trucks, and they took them from one spot to another. They would stop, fire, and move on. That's why it was very difficult to locate the place from where the shell had been fired. And they weren't selective about these spots, whether there were civilians nearby or not. And that fire was sudden. You can't expect such fire, because when there is a spot from -- where there's a recoilless gun or some other weapon, you expect it to fire from there, but when you don't know where they are, then you can't expect the fire, and of course the result is surprise which can lead to success.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I note the time. Perhaps we should make a break now, because the pace was quite fast, or should we continue for five more minutes? Because I want to deal with another brigade and other zones of responsibility and another portion of the map, but we can continue if you so wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is convenient, we'll take a break for half an hour and resume at 5 to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Galic, do you have any problem with the monitor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It's rather good now, but I asked why I cannot see a Serbian transcript. I can only see an English transcript. Or possibly German. I learned some German, but my English is very poor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We have only English transcript during the hearing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, while we're at this map, on the example of this Ilidza Brigade, can you tell us what the goals of the Ilidza Brigade were and what were the goals of the BH Army brigades opposing it?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: The goals of all brigades of the VRS in the zone were the defence of the territory with Serbian majority and the defence of the people living there, not only Serbs but everybody. To what extent that was possible we'll discuss later. And the goals of the forces of the BH Army in the area -- and I must say that in the area of Ilidza, the goal of the Ilidza Brigade of the SRK was to keep the area, which is extremely important because that's where Energoinvest is and water wells, and apart from that, the population there was by majority Serbian. And before June 1992, while we were holding the airport, it connected Ilidza with the other territories controlled by the SRK. That is the airport and further towards Lukavica. And that's why it was important to preserve control over these areas, and through these, you could go north-west and link up with the other forces. That's what the goal of the Ilidza Brigade in the area was. The BH Army, we see that they had strong forces grouped opposing Ilidza. There was a 3rd Motorised Brigade. Later the 101st, then the 101st, and the 5th, 4th, 8th, 9th, and so on. Their goal was to exert pressure on the forces of the Ilidza Brigade in this area which was very small, and advance in the -- along the axis Dobrinja-Alipasino Polje and to link up with the 4th Brigade through the airport. That is, the area toward Igman had to be linked with the other territories controlled by them. That was their goal. We were also under strong pressure for a while from Stup junction toward Ilidza, that is, towards Stojicevac, and further on toward Stup junction. Why? There were some schools there and faculties. So the goal was to take these buildings and drive out the Serbs from these areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now move away from this map and perhaps you could tell us where which brigade was and what the goals, intentions, and tasks of the units belonging to SRK was as opposed to those of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: I think it would be better to use the other map because the Chamber would be able to follow more easily, but if not, I can use this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe that we don't need the exact demarcation lines between the brigades. Who was on the one side and who was on the opposite side, and which forces were on each side? And please indicate the dominant points. If possible, please speak slowly and indicate the areas where the brigades were deployed, and if we can enlarge the picture.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: We said that the Ilidza Brigade was up to the river Dobrinja, then up to the river Miljacka, this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While witness is indicating on the map, could we upload that map on our e-court so that we can follow separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, it's not necessary for you to tell us the boundaries. Just indicate the areas occupied by each brigade.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: The next neighbour to the Ilidza Brigade was the Igman Brigade. The Igman Brigade held the area of Hadzici and Blazuj, to the area of Ormanje and towards Kiseljak, and this is this area here. The next brigade of ours was the Rajlovac Brigade. The Rajlovac Brigade held the area between Rajlovac and Zabrdje, and to the river Miljacka. This external area, I don't know if we have to address that at all or should we concentrate only in the direction of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Only towards Sarajevo, but can you tell us something about the population of the Igman and Rajlovac brigades. Who populated those areas?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: The area of the Igman Brigade was actually the area of Blazuj and Hadzici and that was predominantly a Serb-populated area. As for Rajlovac, it was also populated by Serbs. Opposite the Rajlovac Brigade, and you said that I can start also speaking about the positions of the BH Army, this was held by the 2nd Motorised Brigade, and it was dominant in the areas of Sokolj and Brijesce Brdo, all the way up to Zuc. We can see here how much effort this brigade made with the 1st Motorised to penetrate into the Serb area. You can see clearly from the map because this map shows the movement of Muslim positions vis-a-vis the Serb position. In the legend we saw that we had ten positions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, Your Honour, but can the General be encouraged to speak a little bit more slowly and Dr. Karadzic also to pause before he speaks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Karadzic and Galic must have understood your intervention. By the way, this is a question for Mr. Robinson or

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do we not have our evidence -- map depicting the various -- the brigades of Sarajevo-Romanija Corps' zone of -- area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I think so, yeah. There are some already admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Throughout the Sarajevo-specific court binder map book we find these maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Depicting the areas of responsibility of various brigades of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Going from the rear, map number 32, which dates from 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Have we admitted them all?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll just check with Mr. Reid, but I actually think so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I'll leave it at that. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic -- just a second. Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: The only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Somewhere at line number 16 -- no, no, no. I'm sorry. No, no, no. Everything is in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: The only value of this map is that this is from 1992, when General Galic started to command, and that's showing changes of the line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I understood, but I was wondering whether we have separate map admitted depicting the areas of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, can you please speak slowly and just tell us roughly where the positions of the brigades were in your time?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Both the brigades?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: The 3rd Brigade of the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We are having problems hearing the witness since he's so far away from the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Galic, since you are far away from the microphone, the interpreters are having difficulty to follow you. So could you speak a bit louder and more slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I'll do my best. The next brigade of the SRK was the Vogosca Brigade, which was later merged with the Rajlovac Brigade and the Centar Brigade, and that constituted the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade. It is important to note here that in Vogosca there were huge industrial and commercial potentials that the brigade was supposed to protect. And in Rajlovac we had a repair and maintenance depot called Oro. This --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We didn't hear the witness saying the name of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just -- can we get a wireless microphone? If necessary, we can take a short break. In the meantime, we'll continue. General, could you repeat your evidence from where you referred to some several names of a place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This refers to the disposition of the SRK brigades. In the Vogosca area, we had a large number of industrial and military production facilities, and that was Pretis and Tas. Then in Rajlovac we had a repair and maintenance depot called Oro. Then I said that the Vogosca Brigade and the Rajlovac Brigade and the Centar Brigade were later merged into one single brigade which was named the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade. Let me say something about the BH Army area. We can see here that with respect to this disposition, there is the 1st Mechanised Brigade holding the area towards Zuc up here. I think this is this part here. It's a feature that is overlooking the whole area, and it covers Vogosca, Rajlovac, and the valley of the entire river Bosna. They were holding Orlic, the Vogosca Brigade. I know that there was mention of other brigades such as 112th and other BH Army brigades, but basically this was the area held by [indiscernible] brigades, Bugarsko [phoen], Orlic, and other places. What is interesting here, in view of the disposition of the BH Army, we can see that their zones go all the way to the centre. That's how they're marked. There was no indication of what is the civilian zone and what is the military zone because the brigade zone went all to centre and then we had the area of the next brigade. Now, there's another brigade there, the SRK brigade, and that was the 1st Romanija Brigade. Together with the mixed anti-armour regiment, they were holding the area of Hresa and the general area around it. It was rather difficult terrain in depth, and we can see that there are no -- almost no roads there. When we handed over the airport, I had a very serious problem with the access to this area and our brigades because they were all up there, and the access was only possible from Sumlovac [phoen], Hresa, towards Vogosca, but since there were no roads there we had to build one throughout the whole war and that was a major project. Facing this brigade was the 7th Mountain Brigade. It mainly held Grdonj. The 3rd Mountain Brigade held Pasino Brdo. The 2nd Mountain Brigade held positions between Kozja Cuprija and Pasino Brdo. The 1st Mountain Brigade held position between Velika and Mala Colina Kapa all the way down to Kozja Cuprija. The next one is the 10th Mountain Brigade holding the positions mainly at Debelo Brdo, including Brijesce and the rest of the settlement. One very interesting thing is that the features in this area held by the BH Army between Grdonj, Pasino Brdo and then Velika and Mala Kapa, and then to Debelo Brdo, they separated this area toward Trebevic and Hresa which means that Sarajevo could hardly been seen from the positions of the VRS or it could only be seen from certain positions. The next brigade, first we had the 1st Romanija Brigade holding everything, including Grbavica for a period of time. Later on it was redeployed beyond Grbavica and it held the positions of the SRK. We can see that opposite this brigade in the area of Grbavica was the 1st Motorised Brigade and later on, due to some rearrangement, 105th Brigade came and, according to the information I have, it had a different name as well, and it replaced the Mechanised Brigade. The 6th -- now we have the positions of Sarajevo-Romanija Corps as well. These are the positions held by the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade including the positions between Mravac [phoen] towards Dobrinja, part of Dobrinja, and now depending on -- on the stage of war it held different positions. Initially it held positions until July 1993 towards Jahorina, because that's where the front line was, and later on it focused on this area here which is Grbavica and Lukavica and Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Karadzic, would you like the General to continue to explain on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Excellency. I would just like to ask while he's still standing there, General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was informed that it is possible to install a microphone with wire so that General can speak while standing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We won't be needing it. We have finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you just tell us about this internal front line around Sarajevo. How long was it, the one that held by the SRK?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Well, it varied, but generally speaking, it was around 65 kilometres. And the entire length of the front line of the corps was between 240 and 320 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Within this front line of 65 kilometres --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that now the General can return to his seat.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he can return to his seat. Are we going to admit the whole map? Yes. It's been admitted. Now the General can go back to his seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, you'd inquired about whether or not there were other maps which tended to show the brigade's area of responsibility. We've identified from 1994, P1021, D718; from 1995, D311 and P842; from July 1992, P1494; and from 1994 again, D2788.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I just looked at the Exhibit D718, but since the translation is missing, we have difficulty identifying the name of the brigades. But I'll check with the other exhibits and I'll come back to this issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call up another map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A minute ago you said that the area of responsibility stretched towards the centre.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So can we please have 1D10502.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The zone of responsibility of the BH Army brigades?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. 1D10502, can we just look at the legend, and the date is the 19th of December, 1992; is that correct? In the left corner you can see the dates. Thank you. Can we now see the whole map. Can you read whose map this is? What does it depict?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: This is the layout of disposition of units of the 1st Corps and the -- the staff of the defence of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: District Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please put a pause on your part as well, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, can you please tell us, these coloured portions between the confrontation line and the city, what do they signify, and what is the importance of these portions, and what did the brigades have in those areas with regard to their infrastructure?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I may?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: There's a legend on the bottom right of this map that says what those portions -- those coloured portions might signify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you ask the witness to read out the legend part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, please, would you read this legend out for us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Area of responsibility of the brigades. Two, area of responsibility of the district defence staff of Sarajevo." You see what the symbols are. There where the symbols are similar the colours differ, if you agree with me, although perhaps it's hard to discern. Next it's corps units and this refers to the BH Army units. They have been assigned a yellowish colour. If it's a battalion, then you have two companies at the front end and two companies at the rear end. Next is the unit of the district defence staff of Sarajevo. They were -- these units were also plotted into the map but in the colour green. It's going to be difficult to discern those since the map itself is prevalently green. And that's all that the legend says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the central part again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, does this correspond to your knowledge of the way in which the units covered the town? Is this town accurate -- is this map accurate in your experience?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Well, based on what I've just said in reference to that other map, it does fit into this situation generally. We see that we have the District Staff of Vogosca. That's the staff that I referred to. We see the line facing Jezersko. We said that it was the 7th Brigade -- well, all right. It's the Territorial Defence, as it says here. And we said that there was the 10th Brigade from Debelo hill to Colina Kapa. On the other bank of the Miljacka, in the direction of Grbavica, we have the green marking. It should stand for the Territorial Unit but we know that it was the 10th Battalion. Perhaps at the time it was still recorded as such. So it does generally correspond to the situation as I knew it and as I portrayed it on that map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Did you have any other questions? Should I continue with my answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. What did they have in their area of responsibility from the front end to the rear?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: We can see -- let's start from the brigades. This was something that I knew at the time. In this area, including the 4th Brigade, there were the total of 14 brigades of theirs. Every brigade had three battalions on its strength. If we count the command posts themselves, we will see how many there were. So the first brigade times three to get the battalion posts, and then to get the company post that will be multiplied by three again. Based on the disposition of their units, you can see that they drew battalions and then each of these lines should represent the positions of companies. This isn't a disposition with a layout into a line where you would have all the forces in one line and nothing at the rear. Here you can see that every battalion has its depth and the brigades are the ones that constitute the depth of the corps. This part of the map which depicts the deployment of our forces facing theirs is pretty accurate, pretty accurate. I can't make it out that well, though, on this map, so perhaps my statements can be verified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, when you look at this map, can you tell us what were the positions from which fire was opened on your forces, from infantry fire, mortar fire, artillery fire? What was there at the front end and -- the forward end, and what was there in the depth?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Well, as for the forward line, when it comes to features they held almost all the higher ground. In the first line they would be using infantry weapons. Let's define what infantry weapons are. It includes everything up to and including 120-millimetre calibre. If you take a 120-millimetre mortar, that wouldn't be qualified as infantry weapons anymore. That would already be artillery. So they used all these various weapons, including all systems of fire. What were the axes along which they were the most active? Well, those in the direction of Nedzarici and Dobrinja. There the fire was practically nonstop and I'm talking about the fire coming from the BH Army. Then, as for the Grbavica area, from the position of the skyscrapers on the right bank of the Miljacka because they had a commanding view of the area. They were also active from Debelo and Humsko hills. All of these weapons acted in a synchronised manner. If we speak about infantry weapons, we would point out snipers, rifle -- rifles that could fire shells, et cetera. Another area from which there was intensive fire against our positions was Zuc and Vogosca, that was the axis, the northern part. As well as the Zuc-Rajlovac axis.
