We were able to see on that other map that these were indeed the areas where they were most successful in capturing our territory. One of the important areas that was constantly under attack from them was the axis from Sedrenik to Zlastiste. That's the area under the 10th Mountain Brigade. There were constant incursions and raids and active fire. The same applied to Hresa. There was constant movement of forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Take it slowly, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a moment. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't see the relevance of this line of questioning and the General's evidence to Dr. Karadzic's individual criminal responsibility for any aspect of the Sarajevo component, for example. What's -- what's the relevance of this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think we sat through so much of the Prosecution's case in which they were trying to show that fire that was opened on Sarajevo was indiscriminate and disproportionate and was fired at civilian targets with no military reason, and so General Galic's testimony is trying to lay the basis to show what the military reasons were for the fire that was directed into Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to add anything, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll leave it for the moment, but I see the testimony as talking not about fire directed into Sarajevo but nothing other than fire directed at Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will allow the accused to continue the line of questioning. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, you started telling us about the weapons that they used to fire upon you from their depth. Can you continue?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: As for their depth, they used artillery weapons that were positioned at the foot of Hum, thereabouts. Those were 105-millimetre howitzers. They also fired from tanks in part. There was mortar fire, and, as I've already said, other infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was your response when fire was opened at you from one of those positions? What would be the positions you would be responding from and to what extent?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: When it comes to our response to their fire, it largely depended on the forces that they used to fire upon us. If they used sniper units, because they did have sniper units, whereas the SRK did not, we had some sniper rifles but not sniper units, we tried to return adequate fire. What does it mean, adequate fire? To return fire with the same assets that we had been fired upon if we had those assets. If they opened fire on us from snipers, then we'd use snipers as well or other infantry weapons if we didn't have enough snipers. If they fired upon us from mortars, then although one could return fire from other weapons, the best way to return fire is from mortars. The problem was, of course, to distinguish the various assets and the issue of proportionality. Now, why? If you look at the map and, of course, in reality this would be easier to see, the BH Army units were commingled with civilians, and this applied to the situation regardless of whether we're talking about the more proximate or more distant front. So we applied all those principles when returning fire, especially when we were dealing with an urban area. Primarily we wanted to neutralise as our target the source of fire. So we would open fire at that particular source of fire or pursuant to orders. Everybody had to have orders to act upon. Mr. President, I have to stress here what the steps were that we took in order that we may achieve the adherence to the principles that I've just mentioned. First of all, within the corps, we took a number of measures and activities that would ensure that our return fire was indeed the way it should be. And if you will allow me to, I will list the various steps that the corps had to take.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, tell us who would it be who would issue orders and what sort of orders did you receive? And in what way did you make sure that there was efficiency and proportionality? What was your view of their civilians and casualties? First of all, tell us who could issue orders, what sort of orders did you receive, and what sort of orders did you in turn issued?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Let me take it in this order: I will first speak about the orders that we received and what they contained. So first of all, from the superior command and from you we received orders that all the 1949 Geneva Conventions be adhered to, complete with Protocols I and II. I would then in turn issue such instructions further down the corps, and I think that everyone was aware of this. Of course, one has to bear in mind the fact that we were at war. It is really hard to reach every soldier and to train him, but we did do our best to reach every soldier down the line and convey that order to him. The next order that I would issue would be that the civilians should not be the target of the attack. And the same applied to civilian features, civilian buildings and those that enjoyed protection. Now, given the situation in Sarajevo, how far was it possible to distinguish between soldiers and civilians? We did alert UNPROFOR and others during the war that it was very difficult to distinguish soldiers from civilians because, first of all, not all of the soldiers wore uniforms. Secondly, not all of them carried weapons. Some of them would carry weapons only when they were headed to the front, to the confrontation line. We had information to the effect that they had been using UNPROFOR uniforms, especially those belonging to the French UNPROFOR forces. When we alerted them to this, they said they didn't know. And we said, "Why don't you investigate the information that we have that the other side was doing this?" We also had information that they were using VRS uniforms. Under those circumstances, to be able to distinguish at some distance who a civilian or who a soldier was and to demand from soldiers manning positions to be absolutely certain as to who was a civilian or who was a soldier was quite difficult. Nevertheless, that was the order. I issued such an order, and quite a few UNPROFOR members did concede when they came here that, during the war, if I received information that there were civilian casualties, I ordered that the attack be stopped. We also took steps to protect our civilians as well as theirs by alerting them to the fact that the facilities such as hospitals, schools, daycare centres, education institutions, that they not be used by the BH Army. And we did protest with UNPROFOR, and I believe that UNPROFOR themselves protested with the BH Army against the use of such facilities, because there the problem would arise of how to return fire against such features. One prominent problem was that of the Kosevo Hospital, when mortar fire was opened from that building. On a number of occasions we protested against this practice, this was our duty, but to not much avail. Likewise, UNPROFOR features were used to mask their activities. We lodged our protest on that score as well, but it seemed to fall on deaf ears among those in the BH Army. Furthermore, as soon as I took up my position, I issued an order detailing the use of -- the permitted use of artillery. I always asked that a report on the use of artillery be submitted to the -- to one level up the chain of command. For instance, every brigade had its artillery, as did the corps. So a regiment commander could not issue a task to the artillery to open fire on Sarajevo unless he had been given that order from his superior command. Now, was this always adhered to? Well, it depended on the area. It depended on the forces that were firing upon the SRK. As I've already said, the problem lay in the manoeuvres and movement about the town. It was difficult to discern whether we were returning fire against a military target or whether it was no longer there, because if the asset that had fired upon us was mobile, then it would no longer be on the spot from which it fired. Furthermore, we took measures to spread information about it. We lodged protests with UNPROFOR. In addition to all the intelligence we had from people deserting their ranks and from reconnaissance, they were the ones that were the best source of information for us as to what was going on in the territory of the BH Army, and I think that we will be talking about these protests later. So these were the main measures and activities that we took in order to ensure that the attacks were legitimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did you know where their weapons were deployed and what the source of fire on you was? How did you know that, and how did you control your response?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: The information about their positions, their units, their weapons came mostly from our intelligence work and from our reconnaissance. We got reports from our reconnaissance what had been spotted where and so on. A good way was to get information from people crossing the lines, crossing over from the part of Sarajevo controlled by the BH Army. We would have some 15 to 20 such persons per day coming from the parts of Sarajevo controlled by the BH Army. We, of course, checked the information obtained from them against other information, but mostly it would be accurate. At the time, we were unable to conduct other reconnaissance. There was a little bit of electronic reconnaissance by tapping their communications, and this way we knew from where they were shooting, but there was always a risk involved, because it's impossible to check the reliability of information so obtained, because they may have wanted to trick us, speaking about these things over the radio. So when they say, "Open fire from mortar from position so-and-so," that may be accurate, but it may also be a ruse, and we were unable to tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When did you reconnoiter and how?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Well, you mean in what depth. That would be a better question. According to the deployment of forces, both our and enemy forces, our reconnaissance was limited because the configuration of terrain was bad. There were high buildings blocking our view, and it was difficult to reconnoiter in depth. When the forces were near each other, there were stretches where there was only a war [as interpreted] between our forces and theirs, and then of course it was not a problem to know from where they were shooting. Or if I take Dobrinja as an example, it was easy to tell, but it was always a problem to reconnoiter the depth of their territory. Whether their command post was in one house or another or in a different building altogether, that was difficult to prove because we know it changes always.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Please, again, if the General can be reminded to speak a bit more slowly. And with a transcript correction at page 52, line 13. It should be "wall" rather than "war," and I think that mistake is because of the speed at which the General speaks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's my problem. I speak fast and it's difficult to solve it at this trial, but I will try to adapt to your needs. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, I believe that it's also a matter of interpretation. We see that reconnaissance is mentioned. Do you mean -- really mean reconnaissance or observation?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Well, I mean both. Yes, you have to be in a favourable position to reconnoiter, but of course you can also observe all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are still hearing the interpretation of your first answer, which was not completed. Could you repeat whether it was a reconnaissance or observation? Could you repeat from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it was both reconnaissance and observation. These are two different things. You can reconnoiter by moving, or you can -- forcefully. And observation, that's when you have a position somewhere and you observe what's happening in front of you. But we had both, reconnaissance and observation. Is that a sufficient answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I hope it is. Please explain to the Chamber, while you were observing, where did you respond? Was there retaliation? If they shot at your staff, did you shoot at their staff or how did you respond? What was the direction of your fire?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: The question is clear. I believe it's a pertinent question too. Why? Because the selection of a target in Sarajevo was always a difficult task. We opened fire not on their staff to retaliate, although my staff at Lukavica, where I was on the upper floor, sometimes there would be 20 shells falling over my head, but I never ordered to return fire on the staff of the 1st Corps or the staff of the Supreme Command. I mostly protested to UNPROFOR to stop fire. If that wasn't done, then we would target the source of their fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you always respond, and what was important for your decision when to respond and when not?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: There were a number of factors I took into consideration. There were few decisions of mine to open fire at a certain target. Basically what influenced my decision when and how to respond was the source of their fire. If it was rifle fire, then we responded with rifle fire. But then a problem arose that was difficult to control. For example, in the evening, rifle fire would commence at a section of the front, and then the whole front line would start firing although there was no reason for that. It is very difficult to control from both sides. Now, if that is a response or not is open to discussion because you would hear replies such as: "We say hello this way to each other to show that we're still alive and to celebrate." But it was a problem on both sides. However, mostly we responded in kind. If there was mortar fire, we respond with mortar fire. But there was no incriminate -- there were no incriminated artillery attacks in those annexes 1 and 2. There was only -- there were only mortar attacks that were incriminated, except for one incident but the prosecutor very soon gave up on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you respond to every provocation, to every instance when fire was open at you?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: I must say to the Trial Chamber that it was difficult, but we were pretty much successful not to respond to fire during cease-fires, because if somebody's killing your people and somebody orders you to bear it without returning fire, it is very difficult, but we were successful to some extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were orders about bearing such things issued?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that there were even similar orders from you, especially in a situation when there were cease-fire agreements. Then orders were issued from the highest levels not to open fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Galic, just a minute ago you stated that, I quote: "We were successful to some extent." What did you mean by "to some extent"? Could you clarify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean refraining from opening fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I want to tell you the truth. We were not always fully successful to stop these attacks or, rather, fire in response to enemy fire, but essentially we were successful and sometimes even fully successful in following such an order. That's what I meant. I'm not sure if I was clear enough. For example, if I can continue to clarify some more, after the TEZ agreement there was a cease-fire, and there is no information either from UNPROFOR or from other sources that we opened artillery fire at that time except for some sniping. We were unable to fully control that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'll leave it at that. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Under whose control is the opening of fire from greater calibres, and under whose control the opening of fire from light weapons? And how can you stop an attacked unit from returning fire?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: The control of fire from light weapons was at the level of companies and platoons, and the fire from mortars and artillery was at level -- at battalion level and up, whereas heavy artillery was under the corps. Speaking about sniping, and I've gotten used to the expression, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But I'm saying from the trenches. When there is infantry fire, who controls that, and how can you achieve that the attacked unit does not return fire?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Well, at that time I couldn't influence that because once I get the information about such a thing, it was too late already. The platoon commander and the company commander can directly influence it, but not always the battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before we tender this map, can you tell us, from the southern slopes to the northern slopes, what could be used to open fire from the slopes of Trebevic from Serbian positions at the Muslim positions at Hum and the other way around?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. If we take the zone of defence of the 1st Corps of the BH Army in Sarajevo, we'll see that the size of the area is 20 by 10 kilometres. If I remember well. And then we can see what can be used to fire through that area. If we're talking about rifle fire, when it comes from rifles then it's most times qualified as sniping, but I as a military professional, I don't agree with that terminology because a sniper is a defined term. Rifle fire is successful up to a distance of 400 metres. You can use hand-held rocket launchers --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the General please repeat these distances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you repeat from the distances.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I gave the general ranges. So a sniper with an optical sight that we had and that the BH Army had as well, maybe theirs were more modern, one could be successful up to 400 metres. And you can also be successful up to 800 metres. An ordinary rifle up to 400 metres. A automatic rifle has an even smaller range. Now, mortars have the range depending on the calibre, 62, 82 and 182 millimetres, which means the range between 3 and 8 kilometres. Hand-held launchers, I said about 200 metres. Rifle grenades, between 150 and 200 metres. Recoilless guns, as the ones they had, approximately 800 metres, between 4- and 800 metres. The ones they had and we also had of were of the 82-millimetre calibre.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this map be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please bear in mind the giving -- having some pause after the witness's answer. Please pay attention to the transcript on your part, please. Probably we need a translation. It's better to have translation of the title and the legend separately, although the witness read them out in the courtroom. Do you have any objection, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification pending translation of those parts.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D3383, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we move away this map, what does a BB mean, Mr. Galic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] BB? Look, there are lots of acronyms that we use. Now I cannot remember what it stands for. I cannot translate it for you because there were too many of these abbreviations. Can you please tell me where you found it? It could have been BR?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There are many BBs here. If we zoom in at any part of the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I suppose it's LR.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look all the way to the eastern portion, and we can find BB there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Maybe it's a Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: A Mountain Brigade abbreviation is BBR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How about lesser units?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: A Mountain Battalion, that would be a BB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That sounds plausible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's possible that the BB was that, but if you have an R -- it must be an R there because it would indicate that it's a Mountain Battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you see a BBR on the map and below which with the colour you see BB. So I take it your explanation that it should be a Mountain Battalion sounds --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This means -- I'm sorry. That's their designation. That's how they did it, and that's how they designated a Mountain Battalion. Well, all right. A Mountain Battalion. Because all these units were later abolished, and this term was not in use very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And MB on this map would mean a Motorised Battalion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] MB could be a Mechanised Battalion, but if it is motorised, then it would be MTB, which will differentiate it from the other one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope I gave you an understandable explanation. If I haven't, please ask me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We see both MTB and MB, so thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, speaking about responses, but let me first ask you this: Apart from responses, did you have any artillery preparations or artillery fire targeting the city, and what would be the purpose of those?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Apart from responding to enemy fire, as far as I know, there were no other artillery activities or otherwise targeting the city. Whenever something happened, I always inquired about it and the answer I got was always that that was the response to the enemy action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the Chamber move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did they make any artillery preparations, and what is the difference between their artillery fire and your artillery fire? And I mean the SRK artillery fire.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Their fire, unlike our fire, if they had selected a specific target, they would fire at it several times without any discrimination with regard to whether it was a military or a civilian target. I believe that they wanted to target a military facility but that was not always the case. According to the information and intelligence that we had and on the basis of the orders that we issued, the point was that only military facilities can be a target and that civilian targets are prohibited from being fired at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many infantry attacks you had with the aim of penetrating into the city that involved artillery preparations, and how many of those attacks did they have?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: We saw it on the map. There is this big area heading towards the city, and that was the area of Otes, and this is where we made preparations. If we look at this map here, we can see that they shifted their positions 11 times within one year, and for shifting the positions they had to open fire, and that is why they had more preparation work than we did. And the more active operations with regard to Sarajevo were in the area of Zuc after December 1992, and the improvement of the positions that I indicated in the map that were disturbed sometime in 1993 -- as for the other activities mainly involved fending off their penetrating the areas that I indicated earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was Zuc an urban part of the city?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't. Orlic, Zuc, and other features were under our control for a time, and I went there. There were not too many houses there, at least not close to one another, and Zuc itself was not an urban area, and the next feature was Orlic, which was rather an elevated one, but not many people know of Orlic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can remove the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you responded to their fire, did you take into account the possible collateral damage in terms of injuries and losses incurred by civilians, and how did you treat this issue, the issue of their civilians and possible civilian casualties with regard to targeting a specific military facility that had to be destroyed?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Earlier I said that on a regular basis, whenever we responded to fire coming from the city and the BH Army, we responded to mainly military facilities that fire came from and that posed a threat to us. Now, in a situation where you have a city, how can one calculate, and what right the commander has with regard to proportionality? It is not specified anywhere. Nobody says what proportional response is required. It depended on the objective. If we wanted to destroy or neutralise a target, it was possible to have the civilian casualties as a by-product of such an action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you undertake any precautionary measures with a view to avoiding, or how did you treat this issue and what measures did you undertake in that regard?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, to keep repeating this, but I've spent the morning listening to the French translation just to try and ensure and see how things are keeping up, and there is difficulty because of the speed at which Dr. Karadzic and the General are speaking with one another, and it seems like the only way I can address that is to keep reminding or asking for reminders to be issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've been following the three discussions, the original language, the French translation, and the third language, and I must say that the French booth is doing an extraordinary work. They are even following the discussions live from the courtroom, and I would like to congratulate them for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You will understand under what circumstances our colleague Judge Lattanzi is working. Please put a sufficient pause. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: According to what you know, during the time while you were the SRK commander, did civilian losses occur and did they exceed the justification of military purposes? And to what extent did the civilians suffer as a result of our responses to their fire?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Civilian casualties in Sarajevo, to the extent that I was aware of that and according to the reports that I was receiving at the time and whether this information was correct, all of these casualties were proportionate to the targets that were fired upon. There was some indication that there was sometimes an excessive use of artillery, and that was something that was not entirely possible to control by officers. The losses incurred in Sarajevo, the problem is always who caused these losses. Everybody was saying that these major losses, for example, in the case of Markale, the initial information was this had been done by the Muslim forces. I believe that General Rose said that when he testified here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll come back to Markale because that deserves special attention.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: You asked me about mass losses, and I think that that was one of the examples of major losses that I can give you an answer about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have observers, international observers, posted next to our weaponry, and how many posts were there, if any?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: I was always asking for this contingent of UNPROFOR, that is to say, UNMOs who came over to our side, that they receive the best possible treatment and protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that. Yes, there were exactly 11 observation posts, and I think that there were eight of them on the Muslim side. Practically every piece of heavy weaponry had one UNMO next to it, and they constantly observed when fire was opened and what was happening. I can tell you that I went to see those UNMOs, and it is interesting that I was receiving protests from UNPROFOR, from the Muslim side, whereas the UNMOs on our side never informed me that our weaponry was used not according to plan and without proper purpose.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's P2 -- that's P01431. That's the map of observation posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could these 11 observation posts have covered the artillery and mortar pieces of the brigades and corps, and could there have been fire without them noticing it?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Well, there could have been. They covered all the positions of the various brigade groups, and since they were deployed to the areas of the brigades, they covered the positions of other artillery groups as well. So at least the way they presented it to me, there could not have been such fire without them noticing it. There would be the various sector commanders in Sarajevo, as well as the entire military observers' contingents, and those military observers who were on our side, they were all reliable sources of information, unlike all the others. They were the only ones we could rely upon for information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From the observers who were on the Serbian side, did you receive the sort of formal or informal protests of the sort that they gave to the other side?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Well, I spoke to all of them. I was the sort of person who would receive everyone to the extent I could, and as far as I remember, they never alerted me to the fact that the artillery forces of the SRK were acting in a way that would not have been legitimate. I didn't receive ever information to that effect. As for the SRK on the other side -- or, rather, as for the other side, they would receive information from UNPROFOR and would then lodge protests to UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you received information from the observers who were deployed on the Bosnian side, what would your response be then to that sort of information that the SRK had opened fire, to these allegations?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you that we took very seriously all such allegations that came our way and treated them responsibly. Each and every protest or allegation was checked upon. I made sure that all the allegations behind each and every protest coming from UNPROFOR was checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And to what extent or to what degree were the allegations behind these protests proved to be true or not?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Well, the degrees of accuracy or inaccuracy in war are very difficult to establish, but I can tell you that in the majority of the cases whenever I tried to double-check these allegations, the response was that they were returning the fire because they had been previously fired upon by the enemy or that they had not been opening fire in that period of time at all. That would be your typical two responses that would come up from our units. In that context I believe that UNPROFOR found it hard as well, especially in view of the fact that they only had a handful of observation posts on the side of the BH Army. It was very difficult for them to establish whether indeed a military target was fired upon and whether artillery was involved and what sort of forces had been involved on the side of the BH Army. And there were a great many things that they were doing at that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: They who?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the BH Army. I'm talking about the various problems that were encountered with some commanders, paramilitary groups. There may have been some blood feuds among them. Among their forces there were some settlings of scores where civilian casualties were involved. This was the situation we were confronted with in the war. And I recall clearly that on the 26th of October, 1993, Dusan Topalovic, Caco, was killed. That day was a dangerous day for everyone in Sarajevo, and a sickening one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Excellencies, is it time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break for 45 minutes and resume at 17 past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to follow up on D718 that we were discussing earlier on today, Mr. Reid has helpfully advised me that the translations we were referring to can be found at P5067, 5057, and 5055, and are on maps -- so-called maps 26, 27, and 28 in the map book. So they're on the immediately following pages in the map book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. We have translation of the legends, but I -- shall we upload P1021, which is the original D718. It's difficult to read Cyrillic, the name of the several brigades, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Indeed. I see now, Your Honour, and I apologise for misunderstanding you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So since we are talking about that issue, I wonder whether in co-operation between the parties, whether Prosecution is capable of producing a map with English translation or the -- I can notice SRK, but the others are a challenge, really.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course. I'm sure we can arrange something, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Otherwise we will have to ask the witness to write down in Latin, but if the parties are capable of producing another English version of this map, I'm -- that would be much convenient. Thank you. We can get rid of this map now. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, can we now address this issue, how the issues that you testified about in the previous two sessions concerning documents played out in reality. Let's especially focus on the fire into town.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D01146.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's especially focus on the fire coming into town. This is a document issued by your command, dated the 13th of September, 1992. You speak of the fire that was opened in paragraph 1. And in paragraph 2, you say that you spoke to Grey and that what was discussed was the opening of a new position for the control of heavy weapons in Nedzarici, and then it was said that Grey talked with the Muslim side who sought to have our weapons placed under control, and then they talk about the control of their own. At the same time, they emphasised that considering the losses they have suffered, war is more important to them than weapons controlling humanitarian aid. Do you recall this conversation?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Well, it's been 20 years, and it's difficult to remember each and every other document, but I do recall the conversation with Grey, and I do recall the questions he put to me, and I agree that this is the way it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Put a pause, please. Could you start over again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Below -- or, rather, the latter part of paragraph 2 you say: "We believe that contact UNPROFOR is necessary and helpful." What sort of contacts did you have with UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: I can speak about my personal relationship with them. I can say that our relationship was sincere and respectful. I believed them to be representatives of their countries which were political and military representatives of their countries and respective armies in our region. I believe that they too were in a difficult position. That's why I tried to help them in anyway I could. And it is accurately represented here what I said. I found their contacts very helpful and, especially, if you'll recall when I said that there were quite a few very important pieces of information on the whole that I would receive from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3384, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, the map that depicted the areas of responsibility in different colours was, I believe, admitted? That was 1D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I think we marked it for identification as D3383.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call up 1D01150.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the text be enlarged a bit. It's hard for me to read it. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For the sake of our colleagues in the courtroom, they could have the English version for themselves, and we could place this one here. This is another document from your command, dated the 17th of September, where you say that there was provocative fire and intense fire. And then you say the enemy mounted a strong infantry attack from the direction of Pere Kosorica Square with the support of mortars, anti-aircraft machine-guns from the Viktor Bubanj barracks and Velesici. The fire was directed at Grbavica. You say that the enemy attack was successfully repelled, that one soldier was wounded in combat. And is this indeed the weapons that opened fire from the direction of Viktor Bubanj barracks in Velesici?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Well, this attack on Grbavica, because it's an attack on Grbavica, would happen quite frequently with the support of heavy weaponry. This was especially the case where sources of fire were from the Viktor Bubanj barracks in Velesici, and I can certainly confirm that this is one of the axes of fire intended for the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3385, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D06307. Thank you. Can the English version be placed at the disposal of other participants in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is again a document from your command dated the 26th of October, 1992. It says it was sent out at 1400 hours. How often were there reports for the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Well, there was an operational report that would normally come out in the evening, and then this supplementary one which would come out at around 1400 hours. Although this might be an interim report, because it's the 26th. The date that I mentioned previously when there was that problem -- no, no. Yes, yes. That's it. You go ahead with your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here that a build-up of forces of unknown strength has been observed in the area of Hrasnica and that four tanks were coming down the Igman slope, and this meant that they were coming down into Hrasnica; right?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Yes. They had a couple of tanks up at Igman. I don't know if there were four or -- I don't know about the numbers. We were observing this from the area up from Igman down to Hrasnica and this would particularly have applied to the area that is called Osmice, because that would be the area of Hrasnica, not on the side of the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just to make this clear, when you say Osmice, is that a different place from Osmice at Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Yes, Stijena Baba. When you go in the direction of Pale, that's the place I'm talking about, Osmice. Whereas the other Osmice is when you head from the area of Hrasnica in the direction of Mount Igman. But that's not the main road that goes from Krupac up towards Bjelasnica, no. This is one of the side roads, not the Krupac-Bjelasnica road, and you know it better than me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There were wounded and killed at Hrasnica. You say six dead, 33 wounded, and 70 per cent were civilians. Was this indeed the case?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: The reports that we sent out to the Main Staff could not be doctored in any way or in any way whitewashed, and that's why I'm saying that what is stated here must be the truth. These are heavy losses to have six people killed and 33 wounded in a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that -- all of that before 1400 hours.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3386, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D06317, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's a document issued by your command on the 10th of November, 1992. It's the regular combat report sent out at 1400 hours to the Main Staff. You say that the enemy shelled the centre of Hadzici and that it targeted Famos from Igman with recoilless guns and ZiSes, and they were targeting the barracks from Mojmilo Hill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I haven't risen for about four documents now but I thought it might be timely to make the point I've raised before you before -- previously, that perhaps Dr. Karadzic could avoid reading the content of the document to the witness before asking him the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the previous two sessions I laid a foundation for all these documents. Now I want to ask whether they put up with such fire and why, because here it says that they didn't shoot back and I want to ask him why. I must introduce the document, among others for the public too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure the foundation you laid was one that could be considered sufficient. I will consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to add anything, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think that Dr. Karadzic has done what you've been asking him to do but he didn't do it immediately prior to admitting -- to showing the document, but I don't see why that would necessarily be a requirement. I think he has laid the foundation. If it's necessary, he can ask were there documents which corroborated or which documented the things that you've discussed in the first two sessions and then show him one by one. But if he puts a document like this before him and asks him what's this about, I don't see how he's leading the witness given the previous testimony that the witness has already given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that the foundational question he put in the earlier sessions was such a -- of such a general nature, so the Chamber would be better off if Mr. Karadzic could put some more specific foundational questions as we go by, but we'll see. Let us continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, you say here under item 2: "Our units are at the lines we reached and around Sarajevo we are not opening fire." Why didn't you open fire around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: I must first be reminded if there was a cease-fire at the time, whether there was such an order issued, but we see a problem here in the area of Hadzici, because they were known to open fire at that area often from Igman and other positions. And these recoilless guns -- gun which also fired, the question is whether it is always necessary to respond to such fire, because if in the meantime there was a cessation of hostilities, it is certain that they had to abide by it. But on the whole and in essence, our forces for the most part, irrespective of the existence of an order to cease fire, as we will see later, mostly refrained from firing. Why? I will tell you very openly. Why was it like that? Whenever we responded, whenever we did anything, there was a general outcry. The Serbs are doing this or that. They're killing civilians, et cetera. Although we certainly only targeted only their military targets. That's why we refrained from such activity all the time. I don't know if this was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3387, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned cease-fire agreements a minute ago. How did you implement them, and what did you do with respect to your subordinate units in such cases?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: There were many cease-fire agreements in and around Sarajevo which you know better than I. As far as I remember, there were about 10 cease-fire agreements or so and other agreements during those two years. Those agreements and orders I mostly got from the Main Staff but very rarely from the Supreme Command. Those orders mostly went through the Main Staff of the VRS and less often they came from the Supreme Command, but occasionally they cited the directive of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you abide by those, and did you forward these orders to your subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Before everything else I must say something else. Each agreement had been prepared politically, morally [as interpreted], and so on, in order to implement it. Only then could we start ceasing fire, stopping offensive operations, and so on. I regularly sent out these orders to my subordinate units, and they sent it down the line, down to the last soldier.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D06311, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: May I just say something for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Page 75, line 4, should be politically, military, and so on, rather than "politically, morally, and so on."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What kind of preparations did you mention for the cease-fire agreements?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Political and military.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at the preamble of this document. You refer to the authority of the Presidency of the republic and you order a cease-fire. Look at the first sentence. Through the line of subordination and command make sure there is a complete cease-fire with the HVO forces and the Muslim forces in your areas of responsibility. Was it your practice to issue such orders?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but is there no translation of this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In order for the witness to be able to see the document more easily, we just collapsed the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we get page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to stay on page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: What I said refers to the preamble of my order. It is clear where the order had originated from and it's the Supreme Command. And it says down here based on the agreement signed by, et cetera, and by the authority of the President of Republika Srpska, which means you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we see the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here, the fifth bullet point from the top warns individuals that they may be targeted by snipers with silencers. But what I'm interested in the following: You hold the commanders of brigades and regiments personally responsible for the implementation of this order. It says commanders will be most strictly punished for any violation because the cease-fire has international significance. Was this strictness of yours usual? Were you usually so strict?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: I don't know if I was strict, but I'm sure I was consistent, because when I got an order from my superior command or the Supreme Command, I had to act upon it and appeal to my subordinate officers to act responsibly. That's what I did always. Here I warned them they would be responsible in various ways in case of noncompliance. This also applied to the non-implementation of other orders. I would like to remind you of all sorts of instructions I gave with regard to opening fire. This was my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3388, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that there were a number of agreements. Did you send out an order to subordinate commands for each agreement or was there a general order for all agreements?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: We had to send out orders for each agreement and we got orders for each agreement, because I wasn't involved in negotiating these agreements so I was not in a position to know whether there was one. Only when I got an order from the Main Staff or from you I could react. I wasn't involved in any other way and based on the orders received, I issued such orders. For each agreement there was a separate order and some were even limited in duration.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see 1D06319.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please explain to us this sentence: All your units holding positions toward the city of Sarajevo are duty-bound to abide by the absolute cease-fire and so on. Where else were there positions to which the cease-fire did not apply?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: We only discussed the positions of the corps around Sarajevo, that is, toward the 1st Corps of the BH Army in Sarajevo. However, I said that the front line was 65 kilometres long, and the remainder of the front line was towards Konjic, Visoko, Vares, Olovo, and in the Praca valley. For a while toward Jahorina, too, but that went on until the -- until July 1993. After the Lukavac operation that front line was abolished.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean some cease-fires were valid only for some regions not for the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Given the fact that I phrased this order this way, it is clear that it only applied to Sarajevo but not to other areas. There have been sufficient definitions of these agreements but let me not go into that now. Maybe later there will be an opportunity to discuss that. I mean, the question how either side abided by the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So what remains is only the Ilijas Brigade which did not have positions facing the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Yes. All other -- the Romanija Brigade and others were there too, but only the Ilijas Brigade had its positions toward -- had its position elsewhere toward Visoko and Vares.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3389, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please tell us about the protests. You have already mentioned that there were protests by UNPROFOR. How seriously did you take that and did you respond to them?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: I said from which level the protests came to me. They mostly went through the commander of the Sarajevo Sector, but there were also protests through the military observers. Each of these protests, irrespective of which UN representative submitted it to me or to my subordinate units, had to be seriously considered, and it had to be considered what could be done.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D01864, please. 1D01864. For the other participants please show the English version and do blow this up for General Galic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 28th of November, you reply to Colonel Davout [Realtime transcript read in error "Dvor"], and you say that upon reception of their information, you started investigating in detail. And you say since at Colina Kapa there are no enemy forces, therefore we had no reason to shoot at that position from an anti-aircraft machine-gun. And there's something else I'm interested in. Item 3. Currently we have no aspirations toward Vojnic field and the Olympic housing development, and the positions of the opposing side are such that an infantry attack would have been unsuccessful. And under item 4 you say that the positions of our tanks are such that we cannot shoot at Hrasno hill from there. Fifth, we are strictly abiding by the order of the commander of the Main Staff. What was the content of the protest to which you replied like this?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: In their protest they enumerated all the problems that they perceived, and I replied to that letter of theirs. But now concerning Vojnicko Polje and item 5 and Olimpijsko Naselje that you asked me about, I said that we had no aspirations towards those areas, and in the introductory part I said in which locations we conducted offensive operations in the area of the 1st Corps in Sarajevo. As for the remaining areas, we were never engaged in any operations, nor did we have any aspirations to have these areas attached to the area of responsibility of the SRK. So I think this made it quite clear, and I don't know why there is any mention of an infantry attack of Vojnicko -- on Vojnicko Polje. If you head towards Alipasino Polje and Vojnicko Polje and if you mount an infantry attack on those areas equals a disaster, and that is why we never wanted to attack this area. Now, concerning this part relating to Hrasno Brdo, it -- it is true that it was impossible to fire from our tanks and the positions where they were located.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 2, you apologise and you say that you were under the impression that this information had been presented to them by the Muslim side and that it was a falsehood, and that they had received order to open fire only in self-defence. Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: I believe that I drafted this letter myself. So it is truly how I wrote it, and it is an example of a document reflecting how I treated the protests coming from UNPROFOR. Now, I also wanted to warn them not to take for granted everything that the BH Army or representatives of the Muslims in Sarajevo were telling them. Therefore, after this letter, these commanders came to see me, and I think that we continued our cooperation to the extent that it was required and possible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3390, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just another transcript notation. Page 79, line 8, it should be Colonel D-a-v-o-u, and it's misspelled in the document it should have a t at the end, rather than "Dvor."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you able to notify UNPROFOR, and if so, did you inform them about the violations of cease-fire, and did you inform them about your duty to fire back? Can you tell us briefly how this worked, if there was a violation of cease-fire, what kind of reports did you send back to UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Concerning this process of reporting and co-operating with UNPROFOR regarding the monitoring of cease-fire agreement took place under various circumstances. For a time we had a commission that after the 5th of February, 1994, worked only on establishing the incidents of cease-fire violations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We are still in 1992.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Oh, we are still in 1992. Very well. Whenever we were informed about violations of cease-fire, and pursuant to your orders and the orders from the Main Staff, we sent reports about these violations. I don't know to what extent these reports were acknowledged and accepted, but partially they were. On many occasions I intervened, in 1992, because they were opening fire from the area of the Holiday Inn where the command of UNPROFOR was, and they were using that as a cover for mortars, and I sent protests about -- to this effect on many occasions. So that was something that amounted to the abuse of that area, but I cannot say that we received replies exactly on every occasion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 1D01181. 1D01181.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You see here that on the 6th of December, 1992, you say that in excess of 200 shells fell on Ilidza and Hadzici and caused extensive damage, particularly at Ilidza. And under item 5 you say that you informed UNPROFOR about the violation of the cease-fire and that you responded by firing at firing positions on Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: One could have expected such operations from time to time. I don't know if it was in 1992, but I remember that on one day, 18 to 20 mortars shells fell on one single area. And particularly in the area of Igman there were lots and lots of operations and fire coming from weapons deployed in Vojkovici and other places. Now when I look at this and when I recall everything that had been told to me, this seems incredible, but there were reports confirming that they had enough ammunition for a longer war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This was at 1600 [as interpreted] hours on the 6th of December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this be admitted. I said 1400 hours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's what it says in the letter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D3391, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, can we have 1D01180. It's the same date only at 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your report in which you say that over 300 shells were fired, which means 100 more, and that the damage was huge. You say that you were -- had a shortage of ammunition of this calibre. You said that two soldiers were killed, that nine were wounded, and that 15 women and children were wounded in Ilidza. Did anyone pay attention to this plight of the Serbs? Was this given any kind of publicity?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: It is difficult to answer such a question after this long time, whether this was widely publicised. This is just a document confirming what happened. I don't know whether this was this particular incident when the bus-stop was targeted at Ilidza which resulted in great loss of civilian life, but I remember that this was not broadcast, either on the CNN or any other media outlet, saying that Serbs were killed at the bus-stop. However, if a similar occurrence took place on the opposite side, it would have been covered by all the media, although I was not able to follow all the reports due to the lack of electricity and other hindrances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have this admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3392, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you inform the Main Staff about these reports and about how you were monitoring the conduct of our army?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: The Main Staff was being informed. Are you referring to the protests? I informed them almost regularly about that, because you can see that these reports are addressed to the Main Staff. Whatever you see here is intended for the Main Staff, and they knew what -- everything that was done in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please have 1D01189.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you ever expecting their attacks, and were you aware of their plans?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: I still don't have the document in front of me, but I can give you a general answer to that question. During that time, we received a lot of intelligence about the commencement of various kinds of attacks. Some of them involved shelling, although I'm hesitant to use that term, and I explained to you in what way were we able to obtain this kind of information. Now, concerning their plans for future operations, we had a lot of information from people who managed to escape. Whether they were members of their army or were close to the disposition locations of their troops and once they came across to our side they were able to tell us what was in the offing. Now, this also involved, as I said, reconnaissance, electronic reconnaissance, and other means of obtaining information about possible attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Here, under item 1, it is said that the planned attack has not yet been carried out, which led me to believe that you had some advance information, but you are informing the Main Staff here that the Muslim forces fired at the Croatian forces in the area of Kiseljak and that you think that their intention was to blame us for that attack. You notified the UNPROFOR, and in spite of that, you conducted some checks with our units and you established that they hadn't opened mortar fire at UNPROFOR buildings and the delegates club in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Well, this is a rather major issue to give you a short answer. I must go item by item.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me help you. Were there any instances in which they were playing games by attacking Croats and then accusing us? Did you fight the Croats in Central Bosnia in the area of Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: I understood the question properly, but I have to give you a lengthy answer, and I don't like that. Now, concerning Croats, during my time, I said that we managed to establish good relationships with them, and we were never at war with Kiseljak, as far as I'm aware of. We only had some kind of screen vis-a-vis that area, because we were sure that the HVO would not attack us from this area which was about 18 kilometres towards Kiseljak. However, one of their brigades which was deployed at Stupska Petlja, a Croatian brigade, until a conflict broke out in 1993 between the BH Army and the HVO, they demonstrated tolerance as much as they were able to. I even conducted some so-called internal negotiations to win them over all to our side but that failed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any instances when they were shooting at their own troops or at Croats with the intention of attributing this to Serbs?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: That was not only one occasion. It happened on many occasions that they fired at their own troops and at the Croats in Kiseljak. I can say that the Croatian forces that were in Sarajevo were part of the BH Army, but later on this brigade was transformed. That is why I'm talking only about the area of Kiseljak. So there were provocations coming from the Muslim side in order to portray these attacks as being carried out by us against Croats. They even sometimes attacked their own forces, and we had plenty information about that, sometimes even we had too much information about their firing both at their own troops and their own civilians. If you were to read a book by Lucarevic entitled "Condemned to Victory," you would get an idea about what they were doing, and this was according to his own admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you receive this information at the time or did you learn that from the book?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew about that at the time, and I explained to you how we acquired this intelligence. But as I said, there was too much information stating that they were firing at their own forces and their own civilians. Now, the question was whether that was really probable and possible, and I'm just telling you how I thought about that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is what you meant to say that this sounded incredible?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3393, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the targeting of the bus-stop and the targeting of civilians somewhere in Blazuj, and yet you did not return fire.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D01190?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was the bus-stop easily visible? Was it targeted deliberately or inadvertently?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: We don't have it yet. Can it be enlarged a bit? Can we zoom in on the document to see what it's about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No. This isn't in Blazuj. This is in Hadzici. It's a different incident, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is another incident involving a bus-stop just before the New Year's Eve. This bus-stop was easily visible, just as was the case with the one in Hadzici. I think that almost all the members of the BH Army were familiar with this area, because they were mostly reinforced and manned by people who were locals. They knew where the bus-stops were and the movement of civilians in general. In this instance 16 civilians were injured. I can tell you that Hadzici was a frequent target of attack, as was the local church.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can see that one soldier was killed, a woman civilian was killed, and you also say that the enemy has been provoking continually and firing from all weapons during the visit by Boutros-Ghali. What is your experience in this context?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Well, when it came to visits by prominent figures to Sarajevo, they would normally go to the area of responsibility of the 1st Corps of the BH Army. That's where the Presidency was, with Alija, and all these public figures, from Mitterrand to others. There would always be provocations, and that applied to the visit by Boutros-Ghali. And the attempt was attribute these attacks to the SRK, to send the message of, "Well, you see how we're faring at their hands here." And this was the case every time an important delegation came to visit.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness repeat the last sentence he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic. The interpreters did not hear your last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Of your answer. Can you repeat? You said that whenever there were high-ranking figures visiting, what happened?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Whenever there were important delegations or senior representatives of politicians or military staff, they would always go to the BH Army-controlled part of Sarajevo. So what they did was to try and attribute fire to us, to portray us as -- us being the SRK, as the ones causing trouble in Sarajevo. At that time, we would warn units that they should refrain from any response to any sort of provocative fire, because we expected that there would be some forthcoming.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain why it was that you ordered that there be no fire, because under 2, it says here that all the SRK units have been ordered that in the course of at that day they should be most strictly forbidden from opening fire. Why was this the case?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Well, whenever there were visits of high-ranking officials, I had to issue orders of this sort. If it came to a conflict along the confrontation line, if there was provocation, no one knew how far this incident could escalate and what the consequences might be and whether they would ultimately be helpful for the side of the SRK and the VRS in general, because we didn't have any -- any aspirations to move towards the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is missing from the transcript in my question is that there was refraining from fire despite the fact that there were civilian casualties.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, I did underline this. I didn't simply have the time to read what this document states, but I know that I said that despite these victims, we should refrain from opening fire. And you must know that I did not issue these orders lightly. It was not an easy thing. It was a difficult situation and with serious consequences for the SRK forces as well as the civilians who were within the AOR of the SRK.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And why was that difficult?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Well, for the simple reason that you had to achieve your plan. You had to achieve your goal, and the goal was clear that the Serbian territories in that region be safeguarded. I don't know if this was something that they referred to in the same way in their documents, but in our documents we referred to such actions as step-by-step toward an intervention. What did this mean? This meant that the purpose was to provoke our forces, and since NATO was present there with its aviation flying over the area of responsibility of the SRK on a daily basis and since we knew what the political situation was at the time, especially in terms of the VRS and Republika Srpska, only a small incident was needed in order for NATO aviation to get involved, or we knew that we were sustaining losses, but nevertheless we will refrain from responding to provocations so that we may preserve the territory.
