Otherwise, who could have guaranteed the Serbs and the SRK in the area the ability to defend themselves from NATO in case they intervened or from combined NATO and BH Army forces if it should come to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was the response on the part of civilians and fighters in general to the fact that you had to refrain from fire?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Well, of course they weren't happy about it, but they knew that these -- the sacrifice through these victims, if there should be any, would be necessary. The civilians themselves knew full well why there was no response in such situations. They knew that it would come to peace ultimately. Throughout my time as commander in Sarajevo, I expected that there would be peace in Sarajevo, that there would be demilitarisation. The talks were held, and the negotiations were proceeding at such a pace that we were aware of the fact that peace could be achieved any day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I believe there's something missing from the transcript at page 91, the first four lines. I believe that General Galic referred to territorial exchanges and that Sarajevo should be divided. And perhaps he can confirm that because I don't see it in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There was no division mentioned. The Drina valley was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: The exchanged [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It can be checked.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I heard it in the French translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I didn't hear it in the English, actually, so maybe there's been something missed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we ask the witness to repeat his answer, or could you put your question again, exactly. Shall I put it for you? The question was, Mr. Galic: "What was the response on the part of civilians and fighters in general to the fact that he had to refrain from fire?" Could you kindly repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The response on the part of the civilians and soldiers to the fact that there was no response to the provocations on the part of the BH Army despite there being casualties was such that they were aware of the reasons why we should refrain from firing, and these were the reasons that we explained to them. All of us in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, as well as the civilians in the area, knew that ultimately peace would be achieved in Sarajevo, because there were talks held about Sarajevo at all times and that it should be demilitarised. You will remember that I emphasised that. There was discussion of protected areas, and there were discussions about the exchanges of territory. The VRS held part of Sarajevo for an area in the Drina valley. There were also talks held with a view to reaching peace agreements. We believed that the Cutileiro Plan would be the one. Unfortunately, it never was implemented. So despite all of this, we agreed that this -- that there was not going to be any response on our part in order to reach that goal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that clear now? Can the document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3394, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, you mentioned several times today that the SRK returned fire on firing positions. Can you tell us where most of these firing positions were and where did this huge number of projectiles land? And as I said, where were most of these firing positions located?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Do you mean the SRK fire?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, the SRK fire and the fire on their firing positions.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Well, we were able to see on the various maps including the operational maps what the disposition of the forces of the BH Army in Sarajevo was. We can see that right at the confrontation line there were forces some 1 to 3 kilometres -- at least 1 to 3 kilometres deep within their territory. There were battalion forces, company forces, and forces of lower-level units. So these were the forces that fire was opened upon, and that only happened if there was outgoing fire from those positions targeting the SRK forces. In other words, this happened at the confrontation line or not that far deep into the territory. The approximate depth. What would the approximate depth be in urban terms? Well, up to 500 metres. Over 500 metres we're talking about the sorts of depth where, because of the disposition of streets and high-rise buildings, you're not able to control the situation. As for other positions, we said that they had the positions where they held recoilless guns. They had APC positions, tank positions, and they would open fire from these positions on occasion, although they frequently shifted these positions. We saw what sort of mortar fire there was. Some of the mortars, those that provided support to the brigades along their axes, were stationary mortars. Their positions would mostly in the same area where the other forces were, and they also had mobile mortars. Next, when we were opening fire on their artillery, this could have happened in the area where they were deployed. That would be in the area of Hum or in the area of Igman. It was but rarely that we would respond to their artillery fire down there. It would mostly have happened in the direction of Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D01443.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this extensive answer. I would now like to show you a number of documents relating to precisely what you've been telling us now. Yes, it's the 11th of January, 1993. The document reads that they fired on Milinkladska and Ozrenska streets. These are city streets populated by the Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: One hundred and ten shells from Mojmilo, and they were even a multi -- multiple-rocket launchers. But you say, under 2, upon clearance from the SRK, the unit opened fire on enemy artillery in the area of Mojmilo and Hrasnica. Is this, then, what you referred to when you said that -- you said responded to artillery attacks? And we can see that under 4 we have casualties which are not negligible. There were wounded.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's certainly how it was. We see here from this area from where we were being fired at, we responded by targeting those positions. It isn't easy to tell now whether that was a pinpoint target or a large target. That's why we had to choose the right weapon for our response in order not to hit anything but the area targeted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3395, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please see 1D01448.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is dated the 15th of January, 1993, and it says that one civilian was killed and 13 wounded by artillery fire at Ilidza. And under item 2, it says that the corps units are ready to respond but during the day did not engage in significant combat activity. And then you say under item 3 that there are instances of population leaving the area due to frequent shelling. You also say further down that the soldiers are uneasy about the Serbian delegation agreeing to accept the constitutional principles.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat his last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you repeat your last sentence, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I hurry and then, as a result, lose more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question is: Did the soldiers follow the developments at conferences, and how did they react? This is my question to you.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm waiting for a sign to start replying. I said in my first answer that living and waging war in Sarajevo was hell for everybody involved. We followed all these conferences, all the soldiers, all the civilians, and we wanted them to be successful so that peace is reached in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and especially in Sarajevo. It was equally difficult for both sides. That's why I say that the soldiers followed the developments and the agreements reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In spite of all the damage and casualties at Ilidza, you say that you are ready to respond to possible attacks, but you did not respond after all. Why not?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: At that time it wouldn't have served a useful purpose. I mean, shooting back at the origin of enemy fire. If we see what was hit, these were daily targets of attacks. It wasn't anything new. Both the soldiers and the civilians in the area controlled by the SRK had already gotten used to taking care of themselves, to protect themselves against enemy attacks. There had already been quite a few casualties on our sides -- on our side.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3396, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see 1D25061?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is dated the 24th of January. And your deputy says here that the enemy fired six shells at Ilidza, that there was constant sniping, and under item 2 it says pursuant to the approval of the chief of artillery, the latter fired at enemy positions in the Nabozici area. Other units did not engage in any more significant combat activity. What is this place, Nabozici? Is that some -- is this a downtown area or what?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: We can see where they fired from, from Mojmilo, Hrasnica and other places, whereas we only responded by firing at Nabozici, which is a road. How do I explain that to you without a map? I can draw it. Nabozici is along the road from Ilijas to Vogosca, and from Vogosca to the Niksic plain -- or the plateau, actually. And this is a mountainous area known as Nabozici. So it's above Vogosca and on to Cemerska -- Mount Cemerska. I hope I was able to describe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In other words, Nabozici is --

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC
utterances.text: Outside of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3397, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, before we adjourn or have the rush to adjourn, I just wanted to advise the Chamber, which is something you already know and also we've already informed General Galic, that it's going to be necessary to interrupt his testimony tomorrow morning to hear the evidence of Ljubisav Simic, and that we anticipated General Galic returning to the Chamber around 11.30 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It may depend. Possibly that may be postponed till the third session. Do you understand that, Mr. Galic and Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, sir, I understand that, and I've already grown used to today's pace. Nothing new. It's normal at such trials. And thank you for this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just have a tiny question. I don't really want to be difficult, but I would like to know the following: Will I be able to see General Galic during the breaks? And of course I will not talk about the substance of his testimony. I understand that the Prosecution has already said something about my conduct, but I would like to know whether I would be able to talk to him during the breaks. I know the Tribunal, the Tribunal knows how I behave, but will I be entitled to see General Galic during the breaks without touching upon the substance of his testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any observation, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just by way of clarification, I would assume that Mr. Piletta-Zanin means he's not going to discuss his testimony at all rather than the substance of his testimony. He is not to discuss his testimony with the General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That is my understanding. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I thought that I was clear, and if you have understood what I said, I'm absolutely delighted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As long as Mr. Piletta-Zanin does not discuss about Mr. Galic's testimony, the Chamber sees no difficulty with it. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 16th day of April, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.47 p.m.,
